# AI Voice Agent for a Dental Practice: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-voice-agent-for-dental-practice
Published: 2026-08-17

Direct answer: An AI voice agent for a dental practice is only worth buying if it can hold a real dental call, not the routine cleaning-booking demo every vendor shows, and prove that more of those calls turn into kept appointments once it starts answering. A demo caller who wants a six-month cleaning proves almost nothing; the call that decides the contract is a patient in pain, a recall callback, or a question the front desk would normally answer by looking at the chart.

Key takeaways: Test the agent on a pain call and a recall callback, not a routine booking request, since those two call types expose more than any scripted demo will. Roughly a third of new-patient calls into a dental practice go unanswered, and less than half of the ones that do connect turn into a booked visit (Peerlogic, 2026). Close to 3 in 10 calls into a practice already arrive outside business hours (NextPhone, 2026), and a pain call at 9pm needs more than a message taken for the morning. Medical and dental assistants remain the hardest role to recruit according to nearly half of practice leaders (MGMA, 2025), which is a large part of why dental phones go unanswered in the first place. DSO-affiliated practices are projected to grow from 23% of the U.S. dental market to roughly 39% by 2026 (L.E.K. Consulting), so more dental buyers are evaluating a voice agent for ten locations at once, not one.

Section summaries: A six-point evaluation checklist: run a real dental call describing pain, a broken filling, or swelling instead of a cleaning-booking script; test a hygiene recall callback and confirm the agent recognizes the returning-patient context; confirm live write-back into the practice's actual PMS (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve, Denticon); check the after-hours pain-call behavior specifically, a same-day slot offer versus a next-morning message; require a business associate agreement scoped to the voice channel by name; and test consistency across sites for any multi-location or DSO buyer. A dental voice agent needs logic a generic one misses: recall calls are not new-patient calls, pain calls need triage logic rather than default booking logic, insurance questions need a clear escalation boundary, and multi-location consistency matters more here given DSO growth. Why the phone goes unanswered: the same staffing math that makes medical assistants the hardest role to recruit (MGMA, 2025) hits dental front desks, which often run with one trained employee and no backup, and the call-outcome data confirms it: only 68% of new-patient dental calls get answered and only 42% of those convert to a booking (Peerlogic, 2026), while 28.5% of calls arrive outside business hours (NextPhone, 2026) against Clinekt's own 82% after-hours booking-attempt figure. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a cross-specialty orthopedic proof point (no dental-specific quantitative result exists in canon), turned 263 qualified surgical leads into 159 booked appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, using Clinekt's Inbound and Recall agents.

FAQ digest: An AI voice agent for a dental practice answers the phone, recognizes intent (new patient, recall callback, pain call), and books, reschedules, or cancels directly in the PMS rather than only taking a message. It is the voice-specific slice of a broader AI receptionist deployment, which also covers text and web chat and practice management system integration more broadly. Patients generally accept an AI agent on a pain call when it identifies itself immediately, recognizes urgency, and hands off fast rather than pretending to offer clinical advice. A voice agent does not replace the front-desk team; it absorbs recall callbacks, routine booking, and basic insurance questions so staff handle judgment calls. Multi-location dental groups and DSOs should test consistency, not just capability, across every location on the same phone number pattern.

# AI Software for Orthopedic Practices: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-software-for-orthopedic-practices
Published: 2026-08-18

Direct answer: AI software for an orthopedic practice means four functions working as one system: a front desk that answers and routes every call, scheduling logic that understands subspecialty and visit type, referral capture that turns a fax or portal message into a booked appointment, and reactivation that works the list of patients who never called back. Buying any one function alone solves a quarter of the problem; buying all four as separate, disconnected tools trades one integration headache for four.

Key takeaways: "AI software for orthopedic practices" spans four functions (front desk/phone coverage, scheduling, referral management, patient reactivation), not a single tool. Front-office and medical-assistant turnover, not call volume alone, is the operational driver pushing practices to evaluate this as one category. Roughly two out of three specialty referrals never become a completed visit when nobody owns the follow-up loop, the single largest orthopedic-specific stake in the category. Test subspecialty and visit-type routing specifically, since scheduling logic built for a general primary-care calendar breaks on an orthopedic one. Practices seeing real results run these four functions against the same patient list as one connected system, not as four separate subscriptions.

Section summaries: Four distinct functions get sold under the "orthopedic AI software" umbrella: an AI front desk / orthopedic patient engagement software that answers and routes calls; AI scheduling that books the right visit type by subspecialty, imaging status, referral requirements, and payer authorization; referral management that tracks a referral from arrival to completed visit; and patient reactivation that works the list of patients who have not returned. Three data points explain the current timing: a May 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 357 practice leaders found 29% reported increased turnover, concentrated in reception and medical-assistant roles; a December 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 236 practice leaders found phone access named a top-tier 2026 patient-access priority (22%) alongside no-shows, online scheduling, and wait times; and a study of 103,737 referral scheduling attempts at a large academic health system found only 34.8% resulted in a completed appointment (Patel et al., Journal of General Internal Medicine, 2018). Separately, front-office turnover hit 40% across medical practices in 2022, the highest of any staff category (MGMA, 2023), and 82% of patients try to book care outside a practice's regular office hours. A six-point evaluation checklist: ask which of the four functions a vendor's tool actually covers; test subspecialty and visit-type routing on a real scenario; ask how a referral is tracked from arrival to completed visit; confirm after-hours escalation behavior for anything describing symptoms; check EHR/scheduling-system write-back, not just read access; and ask for a completion number, not an activity number. Most of the category is still sold as point solutions with gaps between tools; Clinekt's Inbound, Recall, and Outbound agents work the same patient record from three directions (inbound calls/referrals, dormant-patient reactivation, and net-new demand) so nothing sits in a gap. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopedic practice running Clinekt's full patient activation system, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single recent quarter, a 60% booking rate, driven by full coverage across calls, referrals, and scheduling rather than any one function in isolation.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic AI software is a category of tools automating front-desk phone coverage, scheduling, referral management, or patient reactivation, individually or as a connected system, with no single standard definition yet. An AI front desk is one function inside the broader category, covering phone/message intake, and does not by itself guarantee scheduling logic, referral tracking, or reactivation. Orthopedic AI software does not replace front-desk staff; it absorbs high-volume repeatable work so staff handle complaints, complex authorizations, and clinical conversations. Orthopedic scheduling differs from general medical scheduling because it has to account for subspecialty, visit type, imaging status, referral requirements, and payer authorization at once. Evaluation and deployment should run as a real pilot against a practice's own call and referral volume over a couple of weeks, with deployment itself measured in days once a vendor is chosen.
